query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Substituting a portion (~5 wt%) of the main metal in the boride phase with chromium and applying a controlled heat-treatment will create a chromium-enriched passivating surface that improves resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: Boride-based component (e.g., Fe2B or similar structure) without any intentional alloying for corrosion resistance in its standard production state.
generation.intervention: Introduce approximately 5 wt% chromium into the boride phase via alloying during fabrication combined with a post-fabrication heat-treatment to promote chromium surface segregation.
generation.conditions: Exposed to molten aluminum under hot-dip aluminum-plating operational temperatures (typically near or just above the melting point of aluminum, ~660°C) and the associated thermal cycling.
generation.structural_mediator: A chromium-enriched surface layer that forms via controlled heat-treatment, altering the interfacial chemistry of the boride.
generation.mechanism: Chromium addition leads to the formation of a stable, passivating oxide (or intermetallic) layer during heat treatment that reduces the active dissolution and interdiffusion between the boride and molten aluminum, thereby enhancing corrosion resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion, evidenced by a longer corrosion onset time or reduced weight loss over a given exposure period compared to the untreated baseline material.
generation.baseline: Boride-based components produced by conventional methods without chromium substitution or specialized heat-treatment, exhibiting standard corrosion rates when exposed to molten aluminum.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected to remain effective as long as the operating conditions do not exceed the thermal limits where the chromium-enriched layer loses its passivity (e.g., at significantly higher temperatures or in more chemically aggressive melts than those encountered in standard hot-dip aluminum-plating processes).
generation.uncertainty: The optimal chromium concentration and heat-treatment parameters need further optimization, and the long-term stability of the chromium-enriched layer under operational cyclic thermal stresses remains to be verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of boride-based specimens: one set with approximately 5 wt% chromium substitution and subsequent controlled heat-treatment, and a control set fabricated via the standard process. Expose both sets to molten aluminum under identical controlled temperature conditions representative of hot-dip aluminum-plating operations. Monitor the corrosion behavior over time.
measurements: Weight loss measurements after predetermined exposure times
Metallographic examination of the cross-section to inspect the formation and continuity of the chromium-enriched layer
Surface elemental analysis (e.g., EDS) to quantify chromium distribution and oxide composition
Time-to-failure or local penetration measurements in the corrosion zone
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the chromium-alloyed specimens do not show a statistically significant improvement in corrosion resistance (e.g., reduced weight loss, longer time-to-penetration, or more robust passivating layer) compared to the baseline specimens under identical test conditions, the hypothesis would be falsified.
